gbs333-aa5279-d1e107.summary: States the question: whether only a proposition per se in the second mode is knowable by science properly so called.

gbs333-aa5279-d1e118.summary: First notandum establishing that 'per se proposition' and 'necessary proposition' are convertible: every necessary proposition belongs to demonstration, either as a conclusion (if it is doubtful) or as a principle (if it is not doubtful or is indemonstrable).
claims: Every per se proposition is necessary and every necessary proposition is per se.
Every necessary proposition belongs to demonstration, as conclusion if doubtful, as principle if indubitable or indemonstrable.

gbs333-aa5279-d1e137.summary: Second notandum: every per se proposition falls into the first or second mode of saying per se, which some authors distinguish thus. In the first mode the predicate signifies nothing really distinct from what the subject signifies, being predicated essentially (a genus or essential difference of what falls under it, or an intrinsic part of the thing). In the second mode the predicate signifies something really distinct from and extrinsic to the subject, as in 'man is risible' or 'God is creative'.
claims: Every per se proposition is in either the first or the second mode of saying per se.
On one account, first-mode propositions predicate something essential to, and not really distinct from, the subject.
Second-mode propositions predicate something really distinct from and not intrinsic to the subject, e.g. 'man is risible', 'God is creative'.
concepts: real distinction of predicate from subject

gbs333-aa5279-d1e196.summary: Presents Grosseteste's (Lincolniensis) alternative way of distinguishing the two modes by causal relation: first mode when the predicate is a cause (intrinsic or extrinsic) of the subject, second mode when the subject is a cause of the predicate. Shows that the two accounts classify the same proposition differently: 'matter is in potency to form' is second-mode on the first account (form is extrinsic to matter) but falls under both modes on Grosseteste's, since form and matter are reciprocally causes. Notes that this applies to affirmatives.
claims: On Grosseteste's account, a proposition is per se in the first mode when the predicate causes the subject, and in the second when the subject causes the predicate.
Under the first account 'matter is in potency to form' is per se in the second mode, but under Grosseteste's it is in both modes, because form and matter are mutually causes.
concepts: Grosseteste's theory of per se modes
matter and form as reciprocal causes

gbs333-aa5279-d1e240.summary: Responsive conclusion: taking science broadly (as distinguished from understanding of principles, covering both propter quid and quia) and demonstration broadly (any syllogistic discourse by which a doubtful proposition becomes evident), it is false that every demonstrable and knowable proposition is per se in the second mode. Some first-mode propositions are demonstrable, e.g. 'every ass is an animal', which can be doubtful to some intellect and be made evident by a syllogism such as 'whatever moves itself is an animal; every ass moves itself'.
claims: In the broad sense of science and demonstration, not every knowable proposition is per se in the second mode.
Some first-mode per se propositions are demonstrable, since they can be doubtful to an intellect and made evident by syllogism.
'Every ass is an animal' can be demonstrated through 'whatever moves itself is an animal'.

gbs333-aa5279.summary: Quaestio 6, a logical question about the objects of strict science, asks whether only per se second-mode propositions are scientifically knowable. Biel first establishes that per se and necessary propositions coincide and all belong to demonstration as principle or conclusion, then sets out two ways of distinguishing the first and second modes of per se predication: by essential vs. really distinct predicate, and Grosseteste's causal criterion (predicate causing subject vs. subject causing predicate), noting how the two classify the same proposition differently. His single responsive conclusion, taking science and demonstration broadly, denies that only second-mode propositions are knowable: first-mode propositions such as 'every ass is an animal' can be doubtful to some intellect and made evident by syllogism, and so are demonstrable.
claims: Per se and necessary propositions are convertible, and all belong to demonstration as principles or conclusions.
Taking science and demonstration broadly, some per se first-mode propositions are demonstrable and knowable, so not only second-mode propositions are scibilia.
concepts: Grosseteste's causal account of per se modes
